newsitem.title: ITALY: Tunisian immigrant drowns trying to reach Italy.
newsitem.headline: Tunisian immigrant drowns trying to reach Italy.

text.p: A 27-year-old Tunisian, one of more than 150 North Africans to try to enter Italy illegally this week alone, drowned after the boat he and 39 others were travelling in sank in rough seas, officials said on Friday.

Police and coastguards, battling Italy's growing clandestine immigration problem, said Tarek Ben Abdelatif swam ashore with his companions after their boat was wrecked on the south of the remote island of Lampedusa between Tunisia and Sicily.
Ben Abdelatif slipped as he clambered onto the rocks, hit his head and fell into the water, where he drowned. Coastguards said they recovered his body on Thursday afternoon.
"We have no idea of how many die -- there are whole boats which quite simply disappear," Salvatore Orami, commander of the coastguards' office in Lampedusa, said in a telephone interview.
He said immigrants used to stick to summertime when the seas were calmer and it was safer to make the crossing crammed into ramshackle 10 metre (30 feet) boats.

Now "clandestini", as they are known, are sailing all year round, leaving officials struggling to turn the tide on a problem that makes Italy unpopular with its European allies who want to tighten external borders against drugs and crime.

Italy's 4,000 km (2,500 miles) of coastline and lax immigration laws encourage thousands of would-be immigrants, mainly from North Africa and Albania, to defy the dangers of the trip and go in search of a better life in Europe.
Orami said a record 1,500 clandestini were picked up in Lampedusa last October and this week's rate of arrivals pointed to "a new phenomenon" after a fall in November and December.

Lampedusa, half-way between Malta and Tunisia, is a favoured back-door entry point for Tunisians, Moroccans and Algerians. For them, its shores are a tempting 70 to 120 nautical miles -- or only 14 hours -- away.
New arrivals are taken to the Sicilian port of Agrigento to be served with largely meaningless expulsion orders.
Even officials say these are essentially just an "invitation" to leave the country within 15 days. Some do -- travelling onto other parts of Europe -- but few go home.
Italy issued 56,015 clandestini with expulsion orders in 1995, the latest year for which figures are available. Just 7,417 complied.
Some estimates have put the total number of illegal immigrants in Italy at 500,000 and rising.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left government appears wary of passing tough new laws for fear of appearing racist, but Interior Minister Giorgio Napolitano has said new rules could be worked out soon.
Nevertheless, the government used a vote of confidence in November to push through parliament a bill to allow 250,000 illegal immigrants to legalise their position.
Orami said a new tactic, introduced in November after talks with senior government officials, was having some success.
Coastguards try to intercept the illegal boats at sea, then contact North African authorities and have them escorted home.
"It's the only efficient tactic," Orami said, adding it had been used successfully nine times.
"It's what public opinion wants," he said.
